<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|320|FUNCTION|}}</noinclude>means <math>[f(z)]^2</math>. This may be verified directly by showing, if <math>\text{R}</math> denote the right side of the equation, that <math>\partial\text{R}/\partial z = \partial\text{R}/\partial t</math>; this will require the use of the differential equation

{{block center|<math>[f_1{}'^{(z)}]^2 = [f^2_1(z)+e_1-e_2][f^2_1(z)+e_1-e_3],</math>}}

and in fact we find

{{block center|<math>\left(\frac{\partial^2}{\partial z^2}-\frac{\partial^2}{dt^2}\right)\log\,[f(z)+f(t)] = f^2(z)-f^2(t) = \left(\frac{\partial^2}{\partial z^2}-\frac{\partial^2}{dt^2}\right)\log\,[f(z)-f(t)]</math>;}}

hence it will follow that <math>\text{R}</math> is a function of <math>z+t</math>, and <math>\text{R}</math> is at once seen to reduce to <math>f(z)</math> when <math>t=0</math>. From this the addition equation for each of the functions <math>\text{sn}(u)</math>, <math>\text{cn}(u)</math>, <math>\text{dn}(u)</math> can be deduced at once; if <math>\text{s}_1</math>, <math>\text{c}_1</math>, <math>\text{d}_1</math>, <math>\text{s}_2</math>, <math>\text{c}_2</math>, <math>\text{d}_2</math> denote respectively <math>\text{sn}(u_1)</math>, <math>\text{cn}(u_1)</math>, <math>\text{dn}(u_1)</math>, <math>\text{sn}(u_2)</math>, <math>\text{cn}(u_2)</math>, <math>\text{dn}(u_2)</math>, they can be put into the forms

{{block center|<math>\text{sn}(u_1+u_2) = (\text{s}_1\text{c}_2\text{d}_2+\text{s}_2\text{c}_1\text{d}_1)/\text{D},</math>}}

{{block center|<math>\text{cn}(u_1+u_2) = (\text{c}_1\text{c}_2-\text{s}_1\text{s}_2\text{d}_1\text{d}_2)/\text{D},</math>}}

{{block center|<math>\text{dn}(u_1+u_2) = (\text{d}_1\text{d}_2-k^2\text{s}_1\text{s}_2\text{c}_1\text{c}_2)/\text{D},</math>}}

{{block center|where <math>\text{D} = 1-k^2\text{s}^2_1\text{s}^2_2.</math>}}

The introduction of the function <math>f_1(z)</math> is equivalent to the introduction of the function <math>\mathfrak{P}(z;\ \omega,\ 2\omega')</math> constructed from the periods <math>\omega</math>, <math>2\omega'</math> as was <math>\mathfrak{P}(z)</math> from <math>\omega</math> and <math>\omega'</math>; denoting this function by <math>\mathfrak{P}_1(z)</math> and its differential coefficient by <math>\mathfrak{P}'_1(z)</math>, we have in fact

{{block center|<math>f_1(z) = \frac{1}{2}\frac{\mathfrak{P}'_1(z)}{\mathfrak{P}_1(\omega')-\mathfrak{P}_1(z)}</math>}}

as we see at once by considering the zeros and poles and the limit of <math>zf_1(z)</math> when <math>z=0</math>. In terms of the function <math>\mathfrak{P}_1(z)</math> the original function <math>\mathfrak{P}(z)</math> is expressed by

{{block center|<math>\mathfrak{P}(z) = \mathfrak{P}_1(z)+\mathfrak{P}_1(z+\omega')-\mathfrak{P}_1(\omega'),</math>}}

as a consideration of the poles and expansion near <math>z=0</math> will show.

A function having <math>\omega, \omega'</math> for periods, with poles at two arbitrary points <math>a</math>, <math>b</math> and zeros at <math>a'</math>, <math>b'</math>, where <math>a'+b'=a+b</math> save for an expression <math>m\omega+m'\omega'</math>, in which <math>m</math>, <math>m'</math> are integers, is a constant multiple of

{{block center|<math>\{\mathfrak{P}[z-\tfrac{1}{2}(a'+b')]-\mathfrak{P}[a'-\tfrac{1}{2}(a'+b')]\}\ /\ \{\mathfrak{P}[z-\tfrac{1}{2}(a+b)]-\mathfrak{P}[a-\tfrac{1}{2}(a+b)]\}</math>;}} if the expansion of this function near <math>z=a</math> be
{{block center|<math>\lambda(z-a)^{-1}+\mu+\sum_{n=1}\mu_n(z-a)^n,</math>}}
the expansion near <math>z=b</math> is
{{block center|<math>-\lambda(z-b)^{-1}+\mu+\sum_{n=1}(-1)^n\mu_n(z-b)^n,</math>}}
as we see by remarking that if <math>z'-b=-(z-a)</math> the function has the same value at <math>z</math> and <math>z'</math>; hence the differential equation satisfied by the function is easily calculated in terms of the coefficients in the expansions.

From the function <math>\wp(z)</math> we can obtain another function, termed the Zeta-function; it is usually denoted by <math>\zeta(z)</math>, and defined by
{{block center|<math>\zeta(z)-\frac{1}{z}=\int_0^\pi\left[\frac{1}{z^2}-\wp(z)\right]dz=\Sigma'\left(\frac{1}{z-\Omega}+\frac{1}{\Omega}+\frac{z}{\Omega^2}\right),</math>}}
for which as before we have equations
{{block center|<math>\zeta(z+\omega)=\zeta(z)+2\pi i\eta,\quad\zeta(z+\omega')=\zeta(z)+2\pi i\eta',</math>}}
where <math>2\eta</math>, <math>2\eta'</math> are certain constants, which in this case do not both vanish, since else <math>\zeta(z)</math> would be a doubly periodic function with only one pole of the first order. By considering the integral
{{block center|<math>\int\zeta(z)dz</math>}}
round the perimeter of a parallelogram of sides <math>\omega</math>, <math>\omega'</math> containing <math>z=0</math> in its interior, we find <math>\eta\omega'-\eta'\omega=1</math>, so that neither of <math>\eta</math>, <math>\eta'</math> is zero. We have <math>\zeta'(z)=-\wp(z)</math>. From <math>\zeta(z)</math> by means of the equation
{{block center|<math>\frac{\sigma(z)}{z}=\exp\left\{\int_0^z\left[\zeta(z)-\frac{1}{z}\right]dz\right\}=\Pi'\left[\left(1-\frac{z}{\Omega}\right)\exp\left(\frac{z}{\Omega}+\frac{z^2}{2\Omega^2}\right)\right],</math>}}
we determine an integral function <math>\sigma(z)</math>, termed the Sigma-function, having a zero of the first order at each of the points <math>z=\Omega</math>; it can be seen to satisfy the equations
{{block center|<math>\frac{\sigma(z+\omega)}{\sigma(z)}=-\exp\,[2\pi i\eta(z+\tfrac{1}{2}\omega)],\quad\frac{\sigma(z+\omega')}{\sigma(z)}=-\exp\,[2\pi i\eta'(z+\tfrac{1}{2}\omega')].</math>}} By means of these equations, if <math>a_1+a_2+\dots+a_m=a'_1+a'_2+\dots+a'_m</math>, it is readily shown that
{{block center|<math>\frac{\sigma(z-a'_1)\sigma(z-a'_2)\dots\sigma(z-a'_m)}{\sigma(z-a_1)\sigma(z-a_2)\dots\sigma(z-a_m)}</math>}}
is a doubly periodic function having <math>a_1, \dots a_m</math> as its simple poles, and <math>a'_1, \dots a'_m</math> as its simple zeros. Thus the function <math>\sigma(z)</math> has the important property of enabling us to write any meromorphic doubly periodic function as a product of factors each having one zero in the parallelogram of periods; these form a generalization of the simple factors, <math>z-a</math>, which have the same utility for rational functions of <math>z</math>. We have <math>\zeta(z)=\sigma'(z)/\sigma(z)</math>.

The functions <math>\zeta(z)</math>, <math>\wp(z)</math> may be used to write any meromorphic doubly periodic function <math>\text{F}(z)</math> as a sum of terms having each only one pole; for if in the expansion of <math>\text{F}(z)</math> near a pole <math>z=a</math> the terms with negative powers of <math>z-a</math> be
{{block center|<math>\text{A}_1(z-a)^{-1}+\text{A}_2(z-a)^{-2}+\dots+\text{A}_{m+1}(z-a)^{-(m+1)}</math>,}}
then the difference
{{block center|<math>\text{F}(z)-\text{A}_1\zeta(z-a)-\text{A}_2\wp(z-a)-\dots+\frac{\text{A}_{m+1}}{m!}(-1)^m\wp^{(m-1)}(z-a)</math>}}
will not be infinite at <math>z=a</math>. Adding to this a sum of further terms of the same form, one for each of the poles in a parallelogram of {{smaller|periods, we obtain, since the sum of the residues A is zero, a doubly periodic function without poles, that is, a constant; this gives the expression of <math>\text{F}(z)</math> referred to. The indefinite integral <math>\int \text{F}(z)dz</math> can then be expressed in terms of <math>z</math>, functions <math>\wp(z-a)</math> and their differential coefficients, functions <math>\zeta(z-a)</math> and functions <math>\log \sigma(z-a)</math>.}}

§ 15. ''Potential Functions. Conformal Representation in General.''—Consider a circle of radius <math>a</math> lying within the region of existence of a single valued monogenic function, <math>u+iv</math>, of the complex variable <math>z, =x+iy</math>, the origin <math>z=0</math> being the centre of this circle. If <math>z=r\text{E}(i\phi)=r(\cos\phi+i\sin\phi)</math> be an internal point of this circle we have
{{block center|<math>u+iv=\frac{1}{2\pi i}\int\frac{(\text{U}+i\text{V})}{t-z}dt,</math>}}
where <math>\text{U}+i\text{V}</math> is the value of the function at a point of the circumference and <math>t=a\text{E}(i\theta)</math>; this is the same as
{{block center|<math>u+iv=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int\frac{(\text{U}+i\text{V})[1-(r/a)\text{E}(i\theta-i\phi)]}{1+(r/a)^2-2(r/a)\cos(\theta-\phi)}d\theta.</math>}}
If in the above formula we replace <math>z</math> by the external point <math>(a^2/r)\text{E}(i\phi)</math> the corresponding contour integral will vanish, so that also
{{block center|<math>0=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int\frac{(\text{U}+i\text{V})[(r/a)^2-(r/a)\text{E}(i\theta-i\phi)]}{1+(r/a)^2-2(r/a)\cos(\theta-\phi)}d\theta;</math>}}
hence by subtraction we have
{{block center|<math>u=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int\frac{\text{U}(a^2-r^2)}{a^2+r^2-2ar\cos(\theta-\phi)}d\theta,</math>}}
and a corresponding formula for <math>v</math> in terms of V. If O be the centre of the circle, Q be the interior point <math>z</math>, P the point <math>a\text{E}(i\theta)</math> of the circumference, and <math>\omega</math> the angle which QP makes with OQ produced, this integral is at once found to be the same as

{{block center|<math>u = \frac{1}{\pi}\int \text{U}d\omega - \frac{1}{2\pi}\int \text{U}d\theta,</math>}}

of which the second part does not depend upon the position of <math>z</math>, and the equivalence of the integrals holds for every arc of integration.

Conversely, let <math>\text{U}</math> be any continuous real function on the circumference, <math>\text{U}_0</math> being the value of it at a point P<sub>0</sub> of the circumference, and describe a small circle with centre at P<sub>0</sub> cutting the given circle in A and B, so that for all points P of the arc AP<sub>0</sub>B we have <math>|\text{U}-\text{U}_0| < \epsilon</math>, where <math>\epsilon</math> is a given small real quantity. Describe a further circle, centre P<sub>0</sub> within the former, cutting the given circle in A′ and B′, and let Q be restricted to lie in the small space bounded by the arc A′P<sub>0</sub>B′ and this second circle; then for all positions of P upon the greater arc AB of the original circle <math>\text{QP}^2</math> is greater than a definite finite quantity which is not zero, say <math>\text{QP}^2 > \text{D}^2</math>. Consider now the integral

{{block center|<math>u' = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int \text{U}\frac{(a^2-r^2)}{a^2+r^2-2ar\cos(\theta-\phi)}d\theta, = \frac{1}{\pi}\int \text{U}d\omega - \frac{1}{2\pi}\int \text{U}d\theta,</math>}}

which we evaluate as the sum of two, respectively along the small arc AP<sub>0</sub>B and the greater arc AB. It is easy to verify that, for the whole circumference,

{{block center|<math>\text{U}_0 = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int \text{U}_0\frac{a^2-r^2}{a^2+r^2-2ar\cos(\theta-\phi)}d\theta = \frac{1}{\pi}\int \text{U}_0 d\omega - \frac{1}{2\pi}\int \text{U}_0 d\theta.</math>}}

Hence we can write {{block center|<math>u'-\text{U}_0 = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{\text{AP}_0\text{B}} (\text{U}-\text{U}_0)d\omega - \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{\text{AP}_0\text{B}}(\text{U}-\text{U}_0)d\theta +</math>}}
{{block center|<math>\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{\text{AB}}(\text{U}-\text{U}_0)\frac{(a^2-r^2)}{\text{QP}^2}d\theta.</math>}}
If the finite angle between <math>\text{QA}</math> and <math>\text{QB}</math> be called <math>\Phi</math> and the finite angle <math>\text{AOB}</math> be called <math>\Theta</math>, the sum of the first two components is numerically less than
{{block center|<math>\frac{\epsilon}{2\pi}(\Phi+\Theta).</math>}}
If the greatest value of <math>|(\text{U}-\text{U}_0)|</math> on the greater arc <math>\text{AB}</math> be called <math>\text{H}</math>, the last component is numerically less than
{{block center|<math>\frac{\text{H}}{\text{D}^2}(a^2-r^2),</math>}}
of which, when the circle, of centre <math>\text{P}_0</math>, passing through <math>\text{A}'\text{B}'</math> is sufficiently small, the factor <math>a^2-r^2</math> is arbitrarily small. Thus it appears that <math>u'</math> is a function of the position of <math>\text{Q}</math> whose limit, when <math>\text{Q}</math>, interior to the original circle, approaches indefinitely near to <math>\text{P}_0</math>, is <math>\text{U}_0</math>. From the form
{{block center|<math>u' = \frac{1}{\pi}\int \text{U}d\omega - \frac{1}{2\pi}\int \text{U}d\theta,</math>}}
since the inclination of <math>\text{QP}</math> to a fixed direction is, when <math>\text{Q}</math> varies, <math>\text{P}</math> remaining fixed, a solution of the differential equation
{{block center|<math>\frac{\partial^2\psi}{\partial x^2}+\frac{\partial^2\psi}{\partial y^2} = 0,</math>}}
where <math>z, = x+iy,</math> is the point <math>\text{Q}</math>, we infer that <math>u'</math> is a differentiable<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
